table.text: The study formed part of a larger longitudinal project examining the effects of incarceration on executive functioning, decision-making, and social cognition. Given the substantial attrition typically observed in longitudinal prison research (Dirkzwager & Nieuwbeerta, 2018; Gonçalves et al., 2016; Hassan et al., 2011; Lennox et al., 2013), large baseline samples were targeted. Specifically, the project aimed to recruit approximately 300 incoming prisoners, 300 outgoing prisoners, and 60 community controls at baseline. The target sample size was informed by several a priori power analyses conducted using G*Power (Faul et al., 2007). First, analyses focusing exclusively on incarcerated participants used a mixed repeated-measures design with two groups (incoming vs. outgoing) and six repeated measurements, corresponding to the combination of the three-level Session factor and the two-level Feedback factor (win vs. loss). Assuming a medium effect size (f = .25) and 95% statistical power, the required sample size was estimated at 28 participants (14 per group). Second, analyses including the community control group to evaluate practice effects used a mixed repeated-measures design with three groups and four repeated measurements, corresponding to the two-level Session factor and two-level Feedback factor. Under identical assumptions, the required sample size was estimated at 45 participants (15 per group).

table.text: The preregistered sample-size target was derived from an a priori power analysis in G*Power (medium effect, f = .25, 95% power). However, G*Power approximates such designs as repeated-measures ANOVAs and misspecifies interactions that combine between-and within-subject factors (Brysbaert, 2019), and confirmatory analyses used (generalised) linear mixed-effects models. Therefore, an additional simulation-based power analysis for the design actually used was conducted. This analysis was not preregistered and was carried out after data collection. To avoid circularity, the effect size was set a priori by convention rather than from the observed estimates. For each candidate sample size, datasets were simulated from a binomial mixed-effects model with the full Group × Session × Feedback structure, a by-participant random intercept, and random slopes for Session and Feedback. Each participant contributed 125 trials per session, aggregated to binomial counts within each participant × session × feedback cell. The highestorder interaction was tested with a likelihood-ratio test comparing the full model against a model retaining all lower-order (two-way) interactions, and power was defined as the proportion of 500 simulated datasets in which this interaction was detected at α = .05. The cohort design evaluated included three groups × two sessions. Assuming a small interaction (odds ratio = 1.5) and moderate between-participant variability in the session change (random-slope SD = 0.4 on the logit scale), 85% power for the highest-order interaction was reached at approximately 30 participants per group. Main effects and lower-order interactions reached 80% power at smaller samples. The achieved samples met this target for incoming participants (n = 61 with complete behavioural data; n = 46 with usable EEG) and for controls (n = 42 and n = 31, respectively), but fell below it for outgoing participants (n = 25 and n = 19, respectively). Because the outgoing group was under-powered, its posterior contrasts are correspondingly wide, and null or near-zero effects in this group are interpreted with caution rather than as evidence of absence.

table.title: Effect of Imprisonment on decision-making under reward and punishment conditions: A Longitudinal EEG Study of newly detained prisoners.
table.research_questions:
•	A recent exploratory study suggested that imprisonment may lead to increased risk-taking after three months (Meijers et al., 2018). However, there is currently no longitudinal evidence on how decision-making processes evolve during incarceration and following release. Therefore, we adopt a bidirectional hypothesis framework.
H1: At the behavioural level, we hypothesize that imprisonment and release may alter decision-making processes under uncertainty, as measured in the bandit task. The primary outcomes of interest will be model-derived parameters capturing core aspects of decision-making. According to the model of best-fit, these may include learning dynamics, sensitivity to reward and punishment, as well as other parameters reflecting choice stochasticity or decision noise. We hypothesize that these latent parameters may either increase or decrease over time across the 8-month follow-up period.
H1.a: During incarceration, incoming prisoners may show longitudinal changes in reinforcement learning parameters. Specifically, they may exhibit a reduction or an increase in learning rates; which may be accompanied by altered sensitivities to reward and punishment. Depending on the direction of these changes, we hypothesize that they will reflect (1) higher impulsivity or risk-taking behaviour, or (2) behavioural stabilization or adaptation to the structured prison environment. Changes may also be observed in parameters capturing noise, indicating shifts in decision consistency.
H1.b: Following release, ex-prisoners may also show bidirectional changes in reinforcement learning parameters. Learning rates and reward/punishment sensitivities may increase, reflecting adaptation to a more dynamic and uncertain environment, or decrease due to stress and instability associated with reintegration. Similarly, parameters indexing choice stochasticity may either decrease, indicating more consistent decision-making, or increase, reflecting greater variability in behaviour.

•	At the neural level, feedback processing will be assessed using EEG markers associated with reward and punishment learning. Punishment processing is indexed by frontal midline theta band power and the feedback-related negativity (FRN), which reflect punishment prediction errors and scale with outcome surprisal (Cavanagh et al., 2010; Chase et al., 2011; Holroyd & Coles, 2002; Williams et al., 2021). Reward processing is indexed by increased delta band power and the reward positivity (Rew-P), which reflect reward prediction errors and are modulated by outcome probability (Holroyd et al., 2008; Sambrook & Goslin, 2014; Walsh & Anderson, 2012).
H2: Given the absence of prior longitudinal research in incarcerated populations, we propose bidirectional hypotheses regarding neural sensitivity to feedback. H2.a : During incarceration, neural responses to reward (delta band power and Rew-P amplitude) and punishment (theta band power and FRN amplitude) may either increase or decrease over time. 
H2.b : Similarly, after release, these neural markers may show either recovery, further attenuation, or continued alteration across the 8-month follow-up period.

•	H3 : Furthermore, individual differences in personality traits related to the Behavioral Inhibition System and Behavioral Activation System are expected to moderate these effects. Specifically, some individuals may show increased punishment sensitivity over time, while others may show a decrease, with similar variability expected for reward sensitivity
•	H4 : Finally, for the outgoing group, the magnitude and direction of post-release changes may be modulated by the duration of prior incarceration, with longer detention potentially leading to more persistent or attenuated effects on decision-making and feedback processing.
table.study_design_overview:
The study is a repeated-measures design with time as a within-subject factor (Baseline, 4 months, 8 months). Participants include both incoming detainees assessed shortly after incarceration and outgoing detainees assessed prior to release, recruited from French and Flemish prisons in Belgium. In addition, a community control group is included to account for repeated task exposure effects, with one 4-month interval re-test only. Incoming participants are recruited within the first three to seven weeks following incarceration, whereas outgoing participants are assessed approximately one month prior to release. All incoming and outgoing participants are followed longitudinally at 4- and 8-month intervals for a total of 3 sessions.
Participants will complete a two-armed bandit task lasting approximately 15 minutes. In this task, participants repeatedly choose between two options (bandits) associated with probabilistic outcomes. The reward contingencies are not explicitly known and must be learned through trial-by-trial feedback. The task is designed to assess decision-making under uncertainty, specifically how participants learn from reward and punishment and how they balance exploration of uncertain options with exploitation of known rewarding options.
Behavioral measures include trial-by-trial choices and reaction times. In addition to descriptive performance metrics (e.g., proportion of optimal choices), computational modeling of behavior will be conducted using reinforcement learning models. Model-derived parameters will be extracted from the model of best-fit, to quantify latent cognitive processes, including learning dynamics, sensitivity to reward and punishment, and decision variability (e.g., stochasticity or lapse processes). Neural activity will be recorded throughout the task using electroencephalography (EEG).
Importantly, repeated task exposure may induce practice effects, such as improved performance, faster reaction times, and more stable model-derived parameters over time, independent of incarceration-related changes. The inclusion of a control group assessed at baseline and one matched interval (i.e. 4-month retest only) allows these effects to be quantified and controlled. Accordingly, longitudinal changes observed in incoming and outgoing participants will be interpreted relative to changes in the control group, enabling dissociation between practice-related effects and incarceration-related cognitive changes.
table.randomization:
The reward structure followed a nonstationary two-armed bandit paradigm in which outcome probabilities varied dynamically over time and were periodically reversed between bandits, such that the option with the higher expected value changed across blocks. This structure was identical across participants.
In addition, several task features were randomized to prevent systematic biases. Specifically, the exact trial-by-trial reward probabilities were generated stochastically for each participant, resulting in unique probabilistic sequences. Furthermore, the color assignment of the bandits was randomized between participants and sessions. And their spatial position (left versus right) were randomized across trials. This ensured that learning was not driven by perceptual or spatial preferences. In addition, this randomization minimized the risk of participants sharing task-related information and attempting to anticipate the advantageous option across sessions, which would not generalize due to the stochastic and nonstationary nature of the reward probabilities.
table.data_collection_procedures:
As part of this study, incoming detainees, outgoing detainees, and community control participants will be recruited. Incoming participants will consist of newly detained prisoners, selected from weekly lists of individuals newly received into custody in French and Flemish prisons in Belgium. Outgoing participants will consist of prisoners approaching release. During recruitment periods, we will aim to approach all eligible detainees and invite them to participate, with recruitment timing adapted to institutional and logistical constraints.
Community control participants will consist of first-year psychology students from Ghent University, recruited via the SONA system. Control participants will complete the same task at baseline and 4-month retest.
Prisoners will be excluded if they were transferred from other establishments, are scheduled for deportation or awaiting extradition (incoming group), or if they have insufficient understanding of Dutch or French, present visual or motor impairments, or exhibit inappropriate behavior toward the researcher.
Baseline assessments (T1) will take place in prison, three to seven weeks after incarceration for incoming participants and prior to release for outgoing participants. Follow-up testing sessions will be conducted at 4 (T2) and 8 months (T3) after baseline assessment. Control participants will be assessed at the first 2 sessions only (4-month re-test).
At each assessment, comprehensive contact information will be collected, reviewed, and updated for detainees, including residential address, mobile phone number, email address, and, when available, social media contact details. Participants will also be asked to provide contact information for alternative contacts (e.g., family members or friends), and to provide consent for these contacts to be used in case follow-up is required and their personal contact information has changed.

table.sample_size:
The final target sample size for this study across all groups (control, incoming and outgoing) is approximatively 30 total participants completing the full study. Considering the high rates of attrition in studies involving prisoners with long periods of follow-up (Dirkzwager & Nieuwbeerta, 2018; Gonçalves et al., 2016; Hassan et al., 2011; Lennox et al., 2013), we seek to recruit 300 incoming and 300 outgoing participants for the baseline assessment. For the control group we only seek to recruit 60 participants at baseline. 
Initial sample size estimates were based on a priori G*Power calculations conducted for repeated-measures designs, using a medium effect size (f = .25) and 95% power. These analyses provided approximate minimum sample-size targets for longitudinal group comparisons, but they were not based on the final Bayesian reinforcement-learning parameter analyses.
For the detainee groups, an initial repeated-measures framework with two groups and three sessions suggested that approximately 28 participants would be required. For analyses including the control group over the shared two-session interval, an additional estimate suggested a required sample of approximately 45 participants. These estimates were used as feasibility benchmarks rather than definitive power estimates for the final computational modeling analyses.
table.sample_size_rationale:
Initial sample size estimates were based on a priori G*Power calculations (Faul et al., 2007), conducted for repeated-measures designs, using a medium effect size (f = .25) and 95% power. These analyses provided approximate minimum sample-size targets for longitudinal group comparisons, but they were not based on the final Bayesian reinforcement-learning parameter analyses.
First, a power analysis was conducted for the incarcerated groups only, including incoming and outgoing detainees. This analysis used a mixed repeated-measures framework with 2 groups and 6 repeated measurements, reflecting the combination of the 3-level session factor and the 2-level feedback (i.e. win or lose) factor. For detecting a medium effect size (f = .25), with 95% power, the required total sample size was estimated at 28 participants (i.e. 14 per group). 
Second, an additional power analysis included the community control group for additional analyses of practice effects. Because control participants were assessed at two sessions, this analysis used a mixed repeated-measures framework with 3 groups and 4 repeated measurements, corresponding to the 2-level session factor and the 2-level feedback factor. Under the same assumptions, the required total sample size was estimated at 45 participants (i.e. 15 per group).
However, this project is part of a larger study for which, keeping all other factors constant, an additional power analysis was conducted focusing on within-subject effects across 3 sessions, with 2 conditions (i.e. each task of the study includes at least 2 conditions), and was performed separately within each detainee group. This analysis yielded a required sample size of 28 participants per group.
The final behavioral analyses rely on hierarchical Bayesian reinforcement-learning models and posterior highest density interval contrasts of model-derived parameters. Because formal frequentist power calculations do not directly map onto this inferential framework, the original power analyses are reported only as approximate recruitment targets. The substantially larger baseline recruitment target was chosen to compensate for expected attrition and to maximize the number of participants contributing usable longitudinal data.
table.measured_variables:
•	The primary behavioral outcome variables will be determined by computational modeling of behavior using reinforcement learning models. Model-derived parameters will be extracted to capture latent cognitive processes, including learning rates and sensitivity to reward and punishment, as well as parameters indexing choice variability (e.g., stochasticity or lapse processes), if they are identified by the model of best-fit. These parameters will serve as key outcome variables for assessing changes in decision-making over time.
•	At the neural level, feedback-locked event-related potentials will be examined, focusing on the feedback-related negativity (FRN) and reward positivity (Rew-P). These components will be quantified following feedback onset and compared between outcome types (win versus loss) and across sessions. 
•	In addition, time-frequency analyses will be conducted to assess theta-band and delta-band power in response to feedback. Theta activity is expected to reflect loss-related processing, whereas delta activity is commonly associated with reward/positive feedback processing. Analyses will compare power as a function of outcome (win versus loss) and across sessions.
•	Reaction time (RT) will be included as a covariate in the analyses, as an index of decision processes (e.g., impulsivity or deliberation), rather than as a primary outcome variable.
•	Demographic variables will be collected, including age, gender, level of education, nature of the offense(s) leading to incarceration, length of incarceration, past criminal records, and socio-economic status.
•	Personality and mental health measures will be included by means of self-reported questionnaires. Participants will rate each item based on its applicability over the preceding four weeks.
•	For incarcerated participants, perception of the prison environment will be assessed at baseline using the Prison Climate Questionnaire (PCQ; Bosma et al., 2020), a validated instrument measuring perceived prison conditions and social relationships within the institution.
•	Following release (from T2 onwards), quality of life will be assessed using the Good Lives Questionnaire (GLQ; Harper et al., 2021), which is adapted to measure well-being and life conditions outside the prison environment.

table.statistical_tests:
Behavioral data will first be analyzed using hierarchical Bayesian reinforcement-learning models adapted from previous work applying computational modeling to probabilistic bandit tasks (Ahn et al., 2017; Aylward et al., 2019). Primary behavioral outcomes will consist of model-derived parameters obtained from computational reinforcement learning models. These parameters will be estimated using hierarchical Bayesian reinforcement-learning models fit separately for each group-session dataset, yielding posterior estimates of both group-level and individual-level latent decision-making parameters.
Group and session differences in these parameters will be assessed using Bayesian posterior contrasts. Specifically, highest density interval (HDI) contrasts will be computed to compare posterior distributions between groups (incoming, outgoing, controls) at each session, as well as within-group longitudinal changes across sessions. This approach allows direct probabilistic inference on parameter differences without relying on null-hypothesis significance testing. Practice effects will be evaluated by comparing longitudinal changes in the control group to those observed in incarcerated and ex-incarcerated groups.
Neural analyses will focus on feedback-locked components associated with reward and punishment processing, including event-related potentials (ERPs), namely the reward positivity (Rew-P) and feedback-related negativity (FRN) amplitudes, as well as delta and theta bands power. Neural outcomes will be analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. Fixed effects will include Group, Session, Feedback (win versus loss), and their interactions. Participant will be included as a random effect, with random intercepts and, where appropriate, random slopes for within-subject factors to capture individual variability.
When significant effects are observed in the neural models, post hoc pairwise comparisons will be conducted using estimated marginal means, with appropriate correction for multiple comparisons. Model assumptions will be assessed through standard diagnostic procedures, including inspection of residual distributions and evaluation of model fit.
table.transformations: Raw EEG data will be preprocessed. We will use a Biosemi 32-electrode EEG system with four external electrodes. Two of the external electrodes will be placed on the left and right mastoids. Data will be acquired using ActiveView software, and subsequently converted to BIDS format. To filter and clean the data, we will use MNE-Python (Gramfort et al., 2013). The data will be re-referenced using the reference electrode standardization technique (REST). Different band-pass filters will be applied for event-related potentials (ERPs) and for time-frequency analyses. For stimulus-locked activity, the baseline will be taken before the stimulus presentation. Since participants will not be placed in a Faraday Cage, a Notch filter will be applied to remove the power line noise at 50 Hz. To remove ocular and muscular artifacts, Independent Component Analysis (ICA). Artifact-related components will be identified using a combination of automatic classification and visual inspection of component topographies and time courses, and subsequently removed.
table.inference_criteria: Behavioural reinforcement-learning parameters will be compared using Bayesian posterior contrasts of group-level parameter distributions. Differences will be interpreted using highest density intervals. Neural outcomes will be analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. For these neural models, statistical significance will be evaluated using a two-sided α level of .05, and post hoc estimated marginal mean comparisons will be corrected for multiple comparisons where applicable.
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
Outliers will be identified at the trial level using a within-participant 2-of-3 rule, combining three criteria: median absolute deviation (MAD > 3), z-score (|z| > 3), and interquartile range (IQR beyond 1.5 × IQR). Trials flagged by at least two of these criteria will be excluded from subsequent analyses.
EEG data will be excluded when excessive artifacts are present. Artifact rejection will be based on a combination of automated detection procedures and visual inspection. Trials contaminated by noise (e.g., due to eye movements, muscle activity, or signal instability) will be removed. Participants contributing an insufficient number of valid trials after preprocessing will be excluded from EEG analyses.
table.exploratory_analyses:
Scores on questionnaires assessing mental health, personality, and quality of life inside and outside prison, assessed using the PCQ and GLQ respectively, will be examined as potential moderators of longitudinal changes in reward and punishment processing. Specifically, these measures will be included as covariates in exploratory analyses to test whether individual differences in prison climate perception, post-release quality of life, and psychological functioning are associated with variability in behavioral parameters and neural markers.
The BIS/BAS scale assesses individual sensitivity to reward and punishment, as well as broader motivational tendencies (Carver & White, 1994). BIS/BAS scores will be used to examine whether trait-level motivational sensitivity moderates longitudinal changes in reinforcement-learning parameters and neural indices of reward and punishment processing. In particular, we will test whether individual differences in behavioral inhibition and behavioral activation predict differential trajectories of reward sensitivity, punishment sensitivity, and associated feedback-related neural responses over the 8-month follow-up period. Although BIS/BAS is generally conceptualized as reflecting relatively stable trait characteristics, exploratory analyses will also assess whether these scores show systematic change across the follow-up period.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 8 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: The study protocol was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (OSF; DOI: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/596QD) and approved by the Ethics Committee of Ghent University (2023-085A).
live_data_statements: Participants were recruited as part of a larger longitudinal project investigating the effects of incarceration on executive functioning and decision-making.
All participants provided written informed consent prior to participation.
Incoming and outgoing participants were recruited from 15 Belgian penitentiary institutions.
Incoming and outgoing participants are collectively referred to as prisoners.
Incoming participants were assessed within four to seven weeks following incarceration (M = 31.4 days, SD = 13.9).
Outgoing participants were assessed shortly before release (M = 19.7 days, SD = 35.0).

To minimize perceived links between the study and the judicial system, informed consent procedures were conducted without prison staff present and participants were explicitly informed that the research team operated independently from both prison authorities and the justice system.
All eligible candidates received oral and written information regarding the study and provided written informed consent.
Participants were reminded that they could withdraw from the study at any time without consequences.
Incoming and outgoing participants completed behavioural tasks with EEG recordings, and questionnaires and received financial compensation (€10 for questionnaires and €10 for experimental tasks).
Control participants completed the behavioural tasks and received course credits.
Control participants were significantly younger than both incoming and outgoing participants, and incoming participants were significantly younger than outgoing participants (all ps < .001).
Groups also differed in gender composition as community controls were predominantly female (34 female, 8 male), whereas incoming and outgoing participants were exclusively male.
Participants completed a probabilistic two-armed bandit task adapted from Aylward et al. (2019) programmed in PsychoPy (Python 3.10).
Participants were informed that their performance would determine a real monetary bonus constrained between €0 and €3.

In addition, because the control group comprised both women and men whereas all incarcerated participants were men, supplementary sensitivity analyses were conducted within the control group to evaluate potential effects of gender on behavioural, computational and neural outcomes.
Because participants were incarcerated 488 individuals, access to potentially identifying data may be subject to ethical and data-489 protection restrictions.
Participants were recruited across 15 penitentiary establishments in Belgium that varied in security level, detention regime, and capacity.
Consequently, substantially larger baseline samples were recruited to ensure adequate statistical power following expected attrition.

Incoming participants were primarily recruited from Brugge (32.2%), Nieuw Dendermonde (27.1%), and Jamioulx (18.6%), with smaller proportions from Tournai (8.5%), Marche-en-Famenne (6.8%), Turnhout (5.1%), and Huy (1.7%).
Outgoing participants were mainly recruited from Ittre (20.0%), Leuven Centraal (20.0%), and Leuze (16.0%), followed by Beveren (12.0%) and Saint-Hubert (12.0%).
Smaller proportions were recruited from Brugge, Hoogstraten, Jamioulx, Marche-en-Famenne, and Ruiselede (each 4.0%).
Percentage of participants recruited from each prison in the final S1-S2 complete sample, separately for incoming (IN) and outgoing (OUT) participants.
Participants were excluded if they had insufficient understanding of Dutch, French, or English, experienced visual or motor impairments, or exhibited inappropriate behaviour towards the researchers.
Participants were also excluded if they had already been approached during a previous incarceration period.
Incoming participants were additionally excluded if their incarceration was expected to be transient (e.g., imminent release, extradition, or deportation).
Outgoing participants were additionally required to have served at least six months in detention prior to the baseline assessment.
To facilitate longitudinal follow-up, participants provided contact details on paper-based forms.
Participants still in prison were contacted through institutional channels, whereas released participants were contacted using the information provided at baseline.
Incoming participants were notified of upcoming follow-up sessions through letters sent via the prison communication system (Prison Cloud) or via institutional intermediaries.
At approximately 3 months post-release, participants were contacted to schedule follow-up assessments.

Control participants were significantly younger than both incoming participants (mean difference = 15.91 years, p < .001, d = 1.82) and outgoing participants (mean difference = 23.83 years, p < .001, d = 2.73).
Incoming participants were also significantly younger than outgoing participants (mean difference = 7.92 years, p < .001, d = 0.91).
Education level was described only for the incoming and outgoing detainee groups because all control participants were university students.
Participants were retained only if they contributed at least 10 valid trials per outcome feedback and at least 30 feedback trials overall.

Because the control group comprised both women and men (34 F and 8 M) whereas all incarcerated participants were men, we could not include gender as a covariate in the full between-group models without confounding it with group.
Participants had up to 4 s to choose one option.

text.text: Imprisonment intends to modify future behaviour partly through punishment.
However, little is known about how incarceration alters reinforcement-learning and decision-making.
This preregistered longitudinal study investigated behavioural and neural changes in reward and punishment processing during incarceration and release.

Newly-incarcerated prisoners (Incoming; n = 61), newly-released individuals (Outgoing; n = 25), and community controls (n = 42) completed a probabilistic reinforcement-learning task at baseline and four months later.
Hierarchical Bayesian computational modelling estimated reward and punishment sensitivities, learning rates, and lapse responding.
EEG measured feedback-related negativity (FRN), feedback-locked frontal midline theta (FMθ), and delta activity during outcome evaluation.
Compared to controls, incoming prisoners exhibited reduced reward sensitivity and learning rate at follow-up, whereas both incoming and outgoing participants showed greater punishment learning.
Only controls showed the expected reduction in punishment learning rate across sessions.
Behaviourally, controls made more optimal choices than prisoners at baseline, although outgoing participants improved to the same level as controls after release.
Neurally, loss-win FRN differentiation strengthened across sessions in all groups.
Delta activity was enhanced in both prisoner groups following reward and punishment, whereas FMθ was elevated overall in incoming prisoners.

Computational and neurophysiological findings jointly indicate that incarceration is associated with alterations in reinforcement learning, characterized by reduced reward learning, sustained reliance on punishment, and altered neural feedback processing.

This shift toward vigilance for negative outcomes may be adaptive within the restrictive prison environment, yet a reliance on punishment information also present after release could shape decision-making during community re-entry and could undermine successful reintegration.

According to reinforcement learning (RL) theories, humans learn by updating their expectations from the rewards and punishments that follow their actions (Rescorla & Wagner, 1972; Sutton & Barto, 1998).
text.formatted: According to reinforcement learning (RL) theories, humans learn by updating their expectations from the rewards and punishments that follow their actions <ref type="bibr">(Rescorla & Wagner, 1972;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Sutton & Barto, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: These principles extend beyond everyday decisionmaking and are embedded in societal systems, including judicial institutions explicitly designed to influence behaviour through consequences.
Imprisonment is partly justified by deterrence, that is, experiencing punishment reduces future offending (Nagin, 2013).
text.formatted: Imprisonment is partly justified by deterrence, that is, experiencing punishment reduces future offending <ref type="bibr">(Nagin, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Despite this rationale, recidivism rates remain substantial across many countries.
A recent global systematic review reported that 18% to 55% of released prisoners are reconvicted within two years (Yukhnenko et al., 2023).
text.formatted: A recent global systematic review reported that 18% to 55% of released prisoners are reconvicted within two years <ref type="bibr">(Yukhnenko et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: These figures fuel ongoing debates regarding the extent to which imprisonment achieves its intended goals and highlight the importance of understanding the neural and cognitive mechanisms through which incarceration may influence future behaviour.
In particular, little is known about how reward and punishment processing changes during incarceration and following release.

Through computational modelling (Daw et al., 2011; Huys et al., 2016), previous research has shown that individual differences in reward and punishment sensitivity can determine how strongly rewards and punishments influence learning and decision-making.

text.text: Importantly, these parameters appear sensitive to both psychopathology and environmental context.

For example, depression and anxiety disorders have been associated with altered learning from positive and negative outcomes (Pulcu & Browning, 2019; Robinson & Chase, 2017), whereas substance use disorders have been linked to abnormalities in reward valuation, punishment responsiveness, and learning (Goldstein & Volkow, 2011; Huys et al., 2016).

text.text: Environmental experiences such as acute stress and exposure to childhood adversity have been associated with such alterations too (Hanson et al., 2017; Kasparek et al., 2023; Lighthall et al., 2012; Nussenbaum & Hartley, 2024).

text.text: As an environment characterized by stress, incarceration represents an important environmental change.
Incarceration involves institutional control, social separation, limited access to rewarding experiences, and exposure to a range of chronic stressors (Liebling & Maruna, 2005; Sykes, 1958).
text.formatted: Incarceration involves institutional control, social separation, limited access to rewarding experiences, and exposure to a range of chronic stressors <ref type="bibr">(Liebling & Maruna, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Sykes, 1958)</ref>.

text.text: These conditions may influence the subjective valuation of rewards and punishments and, consequently, the way individuals learn from them.

Evidence on the effects of incarceration itself remains scarce and has primarily focused on broader constructs such as self-control and risk-taking (Aharoni et al., 2013; Meijers et al., 2018; Mitchell & MacKenzie, 2006).
text.formatted: Evidence on the effects of incarceration itself remains scarce and has primarily focused on broader constructs such as self-control and risk-taking <ref type="bibr">(Aharoni et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Meijers et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mitchell & MacKenzie, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Atypical reward and punishment processing has been reported at the behavioural and neural levels in offender populations (Dillien et al., 2020; Gregory et al., 2015; Murray et al., 2018; Newman & Kosson, 1986).

text.text: However, these studies conceptualize these alterations in reward and punishment processing as stable characteristics associated with offending.
Consequently, it remains unclear whether observed differences in RL and feedback processing reflect the effects of incarceration or preexisting individual characteristics.

To our knowledge, no longitudinal studies have directly examined, at the behavioural and neural level, whether reward and punishment sensitivities change during incarceration or following release from prison.

At the neural level, the feedback-related negativity (FRN) and frontal midline theta (FMθ) activity have consistently been associated with negative outcomes processing, and reward prediction errors (Cavanagh et al., 2010; Holroyd & Coles, 2002; Williams et al., 2021).

text.text: Longitudinal changes in these neural markers have not yet been examined in incarcerated populations and can help identify the neurocognitive mechanisms through which incarceration alters RL, by revealing changes in outcome evaluation and prediction error signalling that are not captured by behavioural measures alone.
The present preregistered longitudinal study investigated how incarceration and release influence reward and punishment processing at both behavioural and neural levels.

Newly incarcerated prisoners ("incoming" group), newly released individuals ("outgoing" group), and community controls completed a probabilistic RL bandit task (Aylward et al., 2019), at two time points separated by approximately four months.

text.text: Computational modelling was used to estimate latent parameters reflecting reward and punishment sensitivity, learning, and value-independent responding.
EEG was recorded during feedback processing, with analyses focusing on the feedback-related negativity (FRN) and oscillatory activity in the theta and delta bands.
The study addressed how reward and punishment processing changes over time during incarceration and following release from prison.
It also aims to distinguish these environment-dependent changes from ordinary practice effects, using a repeated-testing control group.
The prison environment may alter sensitivity to rewards because of restricted access to rewarding experiences.
Likewise, it can lead to increased sensitivity to punishments through repeated exposure to aversive conditions, or, alternatively, lead to adaptation and reduced responsiveness to negative outcomes.
Similarly, reintegration into society following release may again be accompanied by further changes in reward and punishment processing.
Given the absence of prior longitudinal research on RL in incarcerated populations, and the limited and mixed cross-sectional evidence available, bidirectional hypotheses were preregistered.
Behavioural performance was indexed by the probability of selecting the optimal bandit (P(optimal choice)).

text.text: Three feedback-related neural measures were examined.
The FRN and feedback-locked FMθ both index the processing of negative (loss) feedback, whereas delta power reflects the motivational salience of outcomes.

First, the way each group differentiated losses from wins (loss-win contrasts) was examined, followed by how this differentiation changed across sessions, and finally overall group differences in outcome reactivity (delta).
For FRN amplitude, a significant main effect of Outcome, F(1, 85.30) = 15.20, p < .001, was qualified by a significant Session × Outcome interaction, F(1, 1743.39) = 13.37, p < .001.

This loss-related strengthening was significant in incoming participants (Lose S2-S1 = -0.471, p = .035), a nonsignificant trend in outgoing participants (-0.655, p = .065), and absent in controls (-0.070, p = .791).

By follow-up, all three groups showed reliable loss-win differentiation (Table 1; Fig. 5).

text.text: The present study investigated longitudinal changes in RL and feedback processing during incarceration and following release using computational modelling and EEG measures.
Three main findings emerged.

First, behavioural performance and computational modelling provided converging evidence for altered RL processes in prisoners relative to controls, characterized by reduced reward-based learning and sustained punishment-based learning.
Second, both prisoner groups showed globally enhanced delta power to outcomes, indicating altered neural evaluation of feedback.
Third, loss-win FRN differentiation strengthened across repeated testing in prisoners, suggesting an incarceration-related change.
Contrary to our hypothesis, RL parameters showed little longitudinal change.
Lapse responding decreased in all three groups from S1 to S2.

Although this longitudinal change only reached credibility in the larger incoming group, it did not differ credibly between groups, suggesting a common decrease in random responding and greater choice consistency with repeated testing rather than an incarceration-specific change.
The most notable findings emerged from comparisons with controls.
At baseline, controls performed better than both incoming and outgoing participants on the task, and again better than incoming participants at S2.

This behavioural pattern coincided with lower reward sensitivity and learning rates in incoming participants at S2, suggesting that poorer task performance may reflect reduced use of rewarding outcomes to guide future choices rather than a general impairment in learning.
Moreover, both incoming and outgoing participants exhibited higher punishment learning rates than controls at follow-up.
Together, these findings indicate a relative shift towards punishment-driven learning during incarceration.

This pattern is consistent with theories suggesting that stressful environments heighten sensitivity to potential threats and losses, thereby strengthening punishment-based learning while reducing responsiveness to rewards (Browning et al., 2015; Carver & White, 1994; Robinson et al., 2013).
text.formatted: This pattern is consistent with theories suggesting that stressful environments heighten sensitivity to potential threats and losses, thereby strengthening punishment-based learning while reducing responsiveness to rewards <ref type="bibr">(Browning et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Carver & White, 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Robinson et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, these effects emerged despite the absence of credible baseline differences in the computational parameters between groups.
These group differences, present at follow-up but not at baseline, are more consistent with an adaptation developing during incarceration than with a stable, pre-existing characteristic.

However, the results do not indicate a statistically established longitudinal change and the modest longitudinal sample means it cannot be firmly separated from a difference that was simply undetectable at baseline.
The inclusion of a longitudinal control group was essential for distinguishing incarcerationrelated changes from task repetition effects.

Consistent with recent evidence that negative (punishment) learning rates decline with repeated testing (Xu et al., 2025), controls showed a reduced punishment learning rate over repeated task exposure.
text.formatted: Consistent with recent evidence that negative (punishment) learning rates decline with repeated testing <ref type="bibr">(Xu et al., 2025)</ref>, controls showed a reduced punishment learning rate over repeated task exposure.

text.text: Repeated experience may encourage greater reliance on accumulated value representations, making isolated negative outcomes progressively less informative (Chierchia et al., 2023; Lefebvre et al., 2022; Palminteri et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Repeated experience may encourage greater reliance on accumulated value representations, making isolated negative outcomes progressively less informative <ref type="bibr">(Chierchia et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lefebvre et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Palminteri et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, prisoners did not show the practice-related reduction in punishment learning rate observed in controls.
One possible explanation is that adaptation to prison requires sustained vigilance to negative events and behavioural consequences.

Within such environments, punishment-related information may remain highly salient, reducing the typical practice-related tendency to discount negative feedback (Haney, 2012; Zamble & Porporino, 1988).
text.formatted: Within such environments, punishment-related information may remain highly salient, reducing the typical practice-related tendency to discount negative feedback <ref type="bibr">(Haney, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Zamble & Porporino, 1988)</ref>.

text.text: However, this divergence should be interpreted cautiously.

Although punishment learning rate decreased credibly only in controls, the Group × Session contrasts did not reach credibility, so the difference is suggestive rather than established, a limitation associated with the modest longitudinal sample.

At the neural level, FMθ was elevated overall in incoming prisoners relative to controls, consistent with heightened feedback monitoring during adaptation to an unfamiliar and uncertain environment (Cavanagh & Frank, 2014; Cavanagh et al., 2010).
text.formatted: At the neural level, FMθ was elevated overall in incoming prisoners relative to controls, consistent with heightened feedback monitoring during adaptation to an unfamiliar and uncertain environment <ref type="bibr">(Cavanagh & Frank, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Cavanagh et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, loss-win FRN differentiation strengthened over repeated testing.

Loss-related FRN became more negative from S1 to S2, with the loss-related FRN increase reaching significance only in incoming participants, such that all three groups showed reliable differentiation by follow-up.
Larger negative FRN responses are generally interpreted as reflecting enhanced processing of outcomes that are worse than expected (Holroyd & Coles, 2002; Sambrook & Goslin, 2015).
text.formatted: Larger negative FRN responses are generally interpreted as reflecting enhanced processing of outcomes that are worse than expected <ref type="bibr">(Holroyd & Coles, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Sambrook & Goslin, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Because this longitudinal strengthening was only significant in incoming prisoners and a trend in outgoing prisoners, but not present in controls, we cannot attribute it to pratice-related effects.

In addition, it runs counter to the more common observation that feedback-related ERPs attenuate as outcomes become predictable through learning (Bellebaum & Daum, 2008), consistent with the RL account of the FRN (Holroyd & Coles, 2002).
text.formatted: In addition, it runs counter to the more common observation that feedback-related ERPs attenuate as outcomes become predictable through learning <ref type="bibr">(Bellebaum & Daum, 2008)</ref>, consistent with the RL account of the FRN <ref type="bibr">(Holroyd & Coles, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Because the present task involved reversing contingencies, however, outcomes never became fully predictable.
Thus, one possibility is that at re-test participants brought sharper task expectations, so that unexpected losses generated larger PE and a more negative loss FRN (Hajcak et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Thus, one possibility is that at re-test participants brought sharper task expectations, so that unexpected losses generated larger PE and a more negative loss <ref type="bibr">FRN (Hajcak et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: However, because the Group × Session × Outcome interaction did not reach significance, the difference between prisoners and controls was not statistically established, possibly reflecting limited power in the small outgoing sample.
This is best read as a suggestive, candidate incarceration-related change to be confirmed in adequately powered designs.
The shift toward punishment processing observed in incarcerated populations is therefore carried by the computational and delta findings rather than by the FRN.
Both incoming and outgoing participants exhibited greater delta power than controls across outcomes and sessions.
Delta oscillations have consistently been associated with motivational salience, reward evaluation, and RL processes (Cavanagh, 2015; Glazer et al., 2018; Watts & Bernat, 2018).
text.formatted: Delta oscillations have consistently been associated with motivational salience, reward evaluation, and RL processes <ref type="bibr">(Cavanagh, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Glazer et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Watts & Bernat, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, older age was associated with lower delta amplitudes, consistent with age-related reductions in reward responsiveness and motivational processing (Eppinger et al., 2011; Samanez-Larkin & Knutson, 2015).
text.formatted: In addition, older age was associated with lower delta amplitudes, consistent with age-related reductions in reward responsiveness and motivational processing <ref type="bibr">(Eppinger et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Samanez-Larkin & Knutson, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Nonetheless, the opposite directions of the age and group associations make an age-driven account of the delta difference unlikely.

In addition, delta differences were present following both reward and punishment feedback, hence they likely reflect altered processing of outcome salience rather than reward processing specifically (Mei et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In addition, delta differences were present following both reward and punishment feedback, hence they likely reflect altered processing of outcome salience rather than reward processing specifically <ref type="bibr">(Mei et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Although enhanced delta activity was present in both incoming and outgoing participants, only incoming participants exhibited reduced reward sensitivity and reward learning, whereas altered punishment learning was observed in both groups.

This suggests that enhanced neural responses during outcome evaluation are not necessarily associated with more effective behavioural updating, but may instead reflect alterations in how feedback information is processed and incorporated into subsequent decisions (Ernst & Steinhauser, 2012; Xiang et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This suggests that enhanced neural responses during outcome evaluation are not necessarily associated with more effective behavioural updating, but may instead reflect alterations in how feedback information is processed and incorporated into subsequent decisions <ref type="bibr">(Ernst & Steinhauser, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Xiang et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Prior work in offender populations has similarly reported atypical, though heterogeneous, feedback-based decision-making, including altered gain/loss valuation (Pachur et al., 2010), impaired reward and punishment learning (Dillien et al., 2020), and reversal-learning deficits (Dargis et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Prior work in offender populations has similarly reported atypical, though heterogeneous, feedback-based decision-making, including altered gain/loss valuation <ref type="bibr">(Pachur et al., 2010)</ref>, impaired reward and punishment learning (Dillien et al., 2020), and reversal-learning deficits <ref type="bibr">(Dargis et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings extend this literature by showing reduced reward-based learning and relatively greater reliance on punishmentbased learning in prisoners at follow-up.

This pattern is consistent with alterations that may develop during incarceration rather than solely reflecting pre-existing characteristics, though the longitudinal change was not itself statistically established.
Several limitations should be considered.
First, the outgoing sample did not meet power requirements and may have reduced statistical power.
Second, the follow-up period primarily captured early adaptation to incarceration rather than long-term consequences.
Longer longitudinal studies are needed to determine whether these alterations persist, strengthen, or normalize over time.
Third, the control group was not demographically matched to the prisoner groups.
However, the primary purpose of the control group was to quantify practice effects rather than to serve as a matched comparison sample.
Moreover, no baseline difference was observed in the computational parameters, and supplementary analyses indicated that age was not consistently associated with the RL parameters.

Nevertheless, because the computational models were fitted separately within each Group × Session dataset, demographic and prison-related characteristics could not be incorporated directly, so residual confounding cannot be completely excluded.
Finally, high attrition rates may have introduced a bias in the results, due to self-selection of participants with different characteristics.

However, rather than participant disengagement, it was largely driven by practical follow-up constraints, such as anticipated release in incoming participants and difficulties reaching out to the outgoing participants.
Such challenges are common in longitudinal studies involving incarcerated populations, where maintaining contact after release is inherently difficult (Quinn et al., 2018; Stewart et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Such challenges are common in longitudinal studies involving incarcerated populations, where maintaining contact after release is inherently difficult <ref type="bibr">(Quinn et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Stewart et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Future work should integrate institutional and psychosocial variables directly into hierarchical RL models to identify which aspects of incarceration drive changes in learning and neural feedback processing (Schurr et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Future work should integrate institutional and psychosocial variables directly into hierarchical RL models to identify which aspects of incarceration drive changes in learning and neural feedback processing <ref type="bibr">(Schurr et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This study provides the first longitudinal investigation combining computational RL modelling with EEG measures to examine adaptation to incarceration.

Together, these findings suggest a shift in the relative weighting of positive and negative outcomes during value updating, with reduced reward-related learning alongside relatively greater reliance on punishment information.
In parallel, enhanced delta responses further indicated altered neural outcome evaluation in prisoners.

The findings are broadly consistent with theories proposing that restrictive and unpredictable environments promote vigilance towards negative outcomes and increase reliance on punishment-based learning (Browning et al., 2015; Robinson et al., 2013).
text.formatted: The findings are broadly consistent with theories proposing that restrictive and unpredictable environments promote vigilance towards negative outcomes and increase reliance on punishment-based learning <ref type="bibr">(Browning et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Robinson et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Such adaptations may be functional within prison environments, where mistakes can carry substantial consequences and opportunities for reward are comparatively limited (Haney, 2012; Zamble & Porporino, 1988).
text.formatted: Such adaptations may be functional within prison environments, where mistakes can carry substantial consequences and opportunities for reward are comparatively limited <ref type="bibr">(Haney, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Zamble & Porporino, 1988)</ref>.

text.text: However, if these alterations persist beyond incarceration, they may influence adaptive decision-making during community re-entry and thereby affect successful reintegration.

These findings highlight the importance of combining computational and neurophysiological approaches to understand how restrictive environments shape learning and decision-making processes beyond what can be inferred from behaviour alone.

text.text: All participants provided written informed consent prior to participation.
Three groups were included: newly incarcerated prisoners (Incoming), prisoners approaching release (Outgoing), and community controls.
Incoming and outgoing participants were recruited from 15 Belgian penitentiary institutions.
Incoming and outgoing participants are collectively referred to as prisoners.
Community controls (first-year psychology students) were included to estimate practice effects.
Details regarding recruitment procedures and power analyses are provided in Appendix 1.
Incoming participants were assessed within four to seven weeks following incarceration (M = 31.4 days, SD = 13.9).
Outgoing participants were assessed shortly before release (M = 19.7 days, SD = 35.0).
Communication with prisoners was facilitated by prison staff to arrange appointments.

To minimize perceived links between the study and the judicial system, informed consent procedures were conducted without prison staff present and participants were explicitly informed that the research team operated independently from both prison authorities and the justice system.
All eligible candidates received oral and written information regarding the study and provided written informed consent.
Eligibility criteria and retention strategies are reported in Appendices 2 and 3.
Participants were reminded that they could withdraw from the study at any time without consequences.
Incoming and outgoing participants completed behavioural tasks with EEG recordings, and questionnaires and received financial compensation (€10 for questionnaires and €10 for experimental tasks).
Control participants completed the behavioural tasks and received course credits.
The final behavioural sample comprised 128 participants with usable data at both time points, including 42 controls, 61 incoming and 25 outgoing participants.
The final EEG sample included 96 participants with usable data, comprising 31 controls, 46 incoming and 19 outgoing participants.
Descriptive statistics for demographic and incarceration-related variables are reported in Appendix 4.

Procedure and Materials Controls were tested in testing rooms at Ghent University.
Sessions took place in institutional rooms in prison and at participants' homes or other locations at follow-up.
Each session lasted approximately two hours and included five cognitive tasks, including the Bandit task reported here, administered during EEG recording, followed by questionnaires.
Task order was randomized across participants to minimize fatigue and order effects.
Participants completed a probabilistic two-armed bandit task adapted from Aylward et al. (2019) programmed in PsychoPy (Python 3.10).
text.formatted: Participants completed a probabilistic two-armed bandit task adapted from <ref type="bibr">Aylward et al. (2019)</ref> programmed in PsychoPy (Python 3.10).

text.text: Participants were informed that their performance would determine a real monetary bonus constrained between €0 and €3.
On each trial they chose between two slot machines with dynamically changing reward probabilities and received feedback (+€0.25 or -€0.25) after a jittered interval (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: On each trial they chose between two slot machines with dynamically changing reward probabilities and received feedback (+€0.25 or -€0.25) after a jittered interval (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">1</ref>).

text.text: The task consisted of five blocks of 25 trials (125 trials total) and lasted approximately 15 minutes.
Reward contingencies were nonstationary and changed across blocks.
One bandit was associated with a higher reward probability (~70% vs ~30%) and alternated between successive blocks.
To introduce uncertainty, trial-specific reward probabilities were sampled around these block-specific means (SD = .10 for block means; SD = .05 for individual trial probabilities).
Computational modelling was used to estimate behavioural outcomes.

Trial-level choices and outcomes were fit with hierarchical Bayesian RL models in hBayesDM (Stan), separately for each Group × Session to avoid cross-group pooling (Ahn et al., 2017; Aylward et al., 2019).

text.text: Models were compared by leave-one-out information criterion (LOOIC).

The best-fitting model (banditNarm_lapse) included separate reward and punishment learning rates and sensitivities, governing how quickly and how strongly gains and losses updated option values, and a lapse parameter capturing attentional lapses, with choices following a softmax rule.

Group-level posteriors were compared with 95% highest-densityinterval (HDI) contrasts (between groups within each session, and S2-S1 change within and between groups), with contrasts excluding zero considered credible.
Full model specifications and fit are in Appendix 5.
Supplementary analyses examined associations between age and individual-level parameter estimates within each Group × Session (Appendix 6).
EEG was recorded using a 32-channel BioSemi ActiveTwo system arranged according to the international 10-20 layout and sampled at 2048 Hz.
Preprocessing was performed in MNE-Python (Gramfort et al., 2013).

text.text: Briefly, bad channels and noisy segments were identified visually.
Power line noise was removed using notch filters at 50 Hz and harmonics.
Independent Component Analysis (ICA) was used for automatic artifacts removal.
Components were classified using ICLabel (Li et al., 2022; Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019).

Bad channels were interpolated, and data were re-referenced offline using the reference electrode standardization technique (REST; Yao, 2001; D. Yao et al., 2019).

text.text: Event-related potential (ERP) and time-frequency representation (TFR) analyses were performed on feedback-locked epochs.
Cleaned data were filtered between 0.5 and 40 Hz for ERP analyses and between 1 and 40 Hz for TFR, segmented from -2 to 2 s around feedback onset.
Analyses focused on a frontocentral region of interest (FC1, FC2, Fz, Cz).
Trials exceeding an interquartile rangebased threshold (±2 × IQR) on peak-to-peak amplitude, mean activity, or slope were rejected (13.2% for ERPs, 11.3% for time-frequency).
FRN amplitude was quantified as the mean-peakto-mean-peak difference between the P2 (150-220 ms) and the subsequent negativity (220-300 ms), relative to a -300-0 ms baseline.
Single-trial theta (3.5-8 Hz) and delta (1-3.5 Hz) power were extracted 0.1-0.7 s post-feedback from Morlet time-frequency representations z-scored to a -1-0 s baseline (Fig. 2).

Recruitment and Eligibility Criteria.
Participants were recruited across 15 penitentiary establishments in Belgium that varied in security level, detention regime, and capacity.
Recruitment periods differed across institutions due to practical constraints in obtaining access, primarily related to overcrowding and recurrent disruptions within the Belgian prison system.

In particular, data collection was interrupted in April 2024 because of prolonged nationwide prison staff strikes, and access to several establishments remained intermittently restricted throughout the recruitment period.
Recruitment periods and characteristics of participating institutions are provided in Supplementary Table S1-1.

text.text: The study formed part of a larger longitudinal project examining the effects of incarceration on executive functioning, decision-making, and social cognition.

Given the substantial attrition typically observed in longitudinal prison research (Dirkzwager & Nieuwbeerta, 2018; Gonçalves et al., 2016; Hassan et al., 2011; Lennox et al., 2013), large baseline samples were targeted.
text.formatted: Given the substantial attrition typically observed in longitudinal prison research <ref type="bibr">(Dirkzwager & Nieuwbeerta, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Gonçalves et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Hassan et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lennox et al., 2013)</ref>, large baseline samples were targeted.

text.text: Specifically, the project aimed to recruit approximately 300 incoming prisoners, 300 outgoing prisoners, and 60 community controls at baseline.
The target sample size was informed by several a priori power analyses conducted using G*Power (Faul et al., 2007).
text.formatted: The target sample size was informed by several a priori power analyses conducted using G*Power <ref type="bibr">(Faul et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: First, analyses focusing exclusively on incarcerated participants used a mixed repeated-measures design with two groups (incoming vs. outgoing) and six repeated measurements, corresponding to the combination of the three-level Session factor and the two-level Feedback factor (win vs. loss).
Assuming a medium effect size (f = .25) and 95% statistical power, the required sample size was estimated at 28 participants (14 per group).

Second, analyses including the community control group to evaluate practice effects used a mixed repeated-measures design with three groups and four repeated measurements, corresponding to the two-level Session factor and two-level Feedback factor.
Under identical assumptions, the required sample size was estimated at 45 participants (15 per group).

Finally, because the broader project focused primarily on longitudinal within-person change across three assessment waves, an additional power analysis was conducted separately within each detainee group.
Assuming three sessions and two experimental conditions, this analysis indicated a required sample size of 28 participants per detainee group.
Consequently, substantially larger baseline samples were recruited to ensure adequate statistical power following expected attrition.
The prison distribution of participants included in the final S1-S2 completer sample is presented in Supplementary Figure 1-1.

text.text: Incoming participants were primarily recruited from Brugge (32.2%), Nieuw Dendermonde (27.1%), and Jamioulx (18.6%), with smaller proportions from Tournai (8.5%), Marche-en-Famenne (6.8%), Turnhout (5.1%), and Huy (1.7%).
Outgoing participants were mainly recruited from Ittre (20.0%), Leuven Centraal (20.0%), and Leuze (16.0%), followed by Beveren (12.0%) and Saint-Hubert (12.0%).
Smaller proportions were recruited from Brugge, Hoogstraten, Jamioulx, Marche-en-Famenne, and Ruiselede (each 4.0%).
The preregistered sample-size target was derived from an a priori power analysis in G*Power (medium effect, f = .25, 95% power).

However, G*Power approximates such designs as repeated-measures ANOVAs and misspecifies interactions that combine between-and within-subject factors (Brysbaert, 2019), and confirmatory analyses used (generalised) linear mixed-effects models.
Therefore, an additional simulation-based power analysis for the design actually used was conducted.
This analysis was not preregistered and was carried out after data collection.
To avoid circularity, the effect size was set a priori by convention rather than from the observed estimates.

For each candidate sample size, datasets were simulated from a binomial mixed-effects model with the full Group × Session × Feedback structure, a by-participant random intercept, and random slopes for Session and Feedback.
Each participant contributed 125 trials per session, aggregated to binomial counts within each participant × session × feedback cell.

The highestorder interaction was tested with a likelihood-ratio test comparing the full model against a model retaining all lower-order (two-way) interactions, and power was defined as the proportion of 500 simulated datasets in which this interaction was detected at α = .05.
The cohort design evaluated included three groups × two sessions.

Assuming a small interaction (odds ratio = 1.5) and moderate between-participant variability in the session change (random-slope SD = 0.4 on the logit scale), 85% power for the highest-order interaction was reached at approximately 30 participants per group.
Main effects and lower-order interactions reached 80% power at smaller samples.

The achieved samples met this target for incoming participants (n = 61 with complete behavioural data; n = 46 with usable EEG) and for controls (n = 42 and n = 31, respectively), but fell below it for outgoing participants (n = 25 and n = 19, respectively).

Because the outgoing group was under-powered, its posterior contrasts are correspondingly wide, and null or near-zero effects in this group are interpreted with caution rather than as evidence of absence.

Participants were excluded if they had insufficient understanding of Dutch, French, or English, experienced visual or motor impairments, or exhibited inappropriate behaviour towards the researchers.
Participants were also excluded if they had already been approached during a previous incarceration period.
Initially, mental disorders were not an exclusion criterion.
However, participants who experienced active psychosis during testing, who were transferred to a psychiatric unit, who were unable to complete the task, or who were non-compliant were excluded.
In rare cases, prison staff denied participation for security or disciplinary reasons.
Additional eligibility criteria differed by cohort.
Incoming participants were additionally excluded if their incarceration was expected to be transient (e.g., imminent release, extradition, or deportation).
In outgoing participants, follow-up eligibility depended on projected release timing.
For two outgoing participants, release was delayed by up to 6 months and the second assessment was conducted in prison.
For these participants, only the first measure was retained for baseline and they were tested twice outside prison, at 4 and 8 months after release.
Outgoing participants released under a limited detention regime were excluded due to the hybrid nature of this status, which combines both incarceration and community reintegration.
Outgoing participants were additionally required to have served at least six months in detention prior to the baseline assessment.
To facilitate longitudinal follow-up, participants provided contact details on paper-based forms.
Comprehensive tracing details included participants' residential address, mobile phone number, email address, and social media profiles.
When possible, participants also provided contact details for alternative contacts (e.g., relatives, friends, social workers, or services they anticipated contacting upon release).

Similar strategies are commonly used in longitudinal studies involving marginalized or high-risk populations to ensure effective followup (Aitken et al., 2008; Stewart et al., 2021; Teague et al., 2018).

text.text: Researchers ensured that participants understood how their secondary contacts' details would be used and that sensitive information, such as their criminal history, would not be disclosed to these individuals.
Several retention strategies were employed to maintain participant engagement throughout the follow-up period.
Participants still in prison were contacted through institutional channels, whereas released participants were contacted using the information provided at baseline.
When possible, participants transferred to another prison or re-incarcerated during follow-up were traced through the national penitentiary database (SIDIS) and reassessed in their new institution.
Participants could withdraw at any time without consequences.
Incoming participants were notified of upcoming follow-up sessions through letters sent via the prison communication system (Prison Cloud) or via institutional intermediaries.
This allowed participants who were employed within the prison to request time off or schedule testing outside of working hours.
During ongoing recruitment periods, participants eligible for follow-up were also contacted directly on recruitment days to confirm their continued interest and availability.

Participants transferred to a different penitentiary institution were identified through the SIDIS penitentiary database, and authorization to conduct testing in the new institution was obtained from the Belgian Federal Public Service Justice (Direction générale EPI -Établissements pénitentiaires).

Participants who were scheduled for release within three weeks following baseline testing were asked to provide contact information, including a telephone number, email address, and/or residential address.
When available, contact details of a social worker, community center, or health service were also recorded.
At approximately 3 months post-release, participants were contacted to schedule follow-up assessments.
If initial contact attempts were unsuccessful, up to three follow-up messages were sent.
For participants who could not be reached through the provided contact information, secondary contacts were used to obtain updated contact details when available.
Letters were also sent to participants' last known residential address.
Participants who were re-incarcerated during the follow-up period were identified through the SIDIS database, provided they had consented to this monitoring in the informed consent procedure.
Participants who were re-incarcerated before S2 were excluded from follow-up analyses, whereas those re-incarcerated between S2 and S3 remained eligible for the final assessment.

It tracks the value of each option separately for rewards and punishments and updates these values trial by trial as outcomes are received.

Learning from rewards and from punishments was governed by separate learning rates (Arew and Apun), and the impact of each reward and punishment was scaled by separate sensitivity parameters (R and P).

Choices were modelled with a softmax rule applied to the combined reward and punishment values, and a lapse parameter (ξ) allowed a proportion of responses to be made at random, independently of learned value.
Learning rates and the lapse parameter were bounded between 0 and 1, and the reward and punishment sensitivities between 0 and 30.
Models that omitted separate reward and punishment sensitivities or included only learning-rate parameters performed substantially worse.
Posterior group-level parameter distributions from the winning model were compared using 95% highest density interval (HDI) contrasts.
For each comparison, posterior samples were subtracted to obtain a distribution of parameter differences, from which the 95% HDI was calculated.

Between-group contrasts were computed separately within each session, longitudinal changes were estimated as S2 -S1 contrasts within each group, and group differences in longitudinal change were evaluated using contrasts of posterior session effects, analogous to a Bayesian difference-in-differences approach.
Following Kruschke (2014) and Aylward et al. (2019), a contrast was considered meaningful when the 95% HDI excluded zero.

Between-subject spread differed markedly across parameters.

The reward learning rate (Arew), reward sensitivity (R) and punishment sensitivity (P) showed substantial individual variation, whereas the punishment learning rate (Apun) and lapse (ξ) were strongly shrunk toward the group mean (across-subject SD ≈ 0.004-0.02).

Because Arew lies on the same (0, 1) scale as Apun and ξ yet varied widely (≈ 0.05-0.95), this narrow spread reflects weak individual-level identifiability as there were few loss trials to inform Apun, and lapse estimates lie near zero.
Individual differences in Apun and ξ should therefore be interpreted with caution.
Inference for these parameters is most reliable at the group level.

EEG was recorded during task performance using a 32-channel BioSemi ActiveTwo system arranged according to the international 10-20 system and sampled at 2048 Hz.
External electrodes were used to record mastoid activity.
Raw EEG data were acquired with ActiveView software and converted to BIDS format.
EEG preprocessing was conducted in MNE-Python (Gramfort et al., 2013).

text.text: Raw files were first inspected to verify recording quality.
For ICA-based artefact correction, a copy of the raw data was band-pass filtered between 1 and 30 Hz using an IIR filter.
Powerline noise was attenuated using notch filters at 50 Hz and harmonics up to 250 Hz.
Independent Component Analysis was then applied using previously estimated ICA decompositions, and components were classified using ICLabel (Li et al., 2022; Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019).

text.text: ERP and time-frequency analyses were performed on feedback-locked epochs on frontocentral electrodes Fz, Cz, FC1 and FC2.
These sites were selected because feedback-related frontal-midline activity is maximal over medial frontocentral cortex.

Indeed, the feedback-related negativity (FRN) and feedback-locked theta and delta responses consistently peak at these electrodes, consistent with a putative generator in the anterior cingulate/medial frontal cortex (Cavanagh & Frank, 2014; Cohen, 2014; Holroyd & Coles, 2002; Sambrook & Goslin, 2015).
