text.text: For ERP analyses, cleaned continuous data were band-pass filtered between 0.5 and 40 Hz and segmented into epochs from -2 to 2 s relative to feedback onset.
Epochs were baselinecorrected using the -300 to 0 ms pre-feedback interval and cropped from -300 to 600 ms for analysis.
Automated epoch rejection was applied over the -1.5 to 1 s window using the electrodes of interest only.
Trials were rejected when identified as outliers on peak-to-peak amplitude, mean amplitude, or signal slope.
For each participant and electrode, trials exceeding an interquartile-range threshold (±2 × IQR) on any metric were rejected.
On average, 13.2% of ERP epochs were rejected, with comparable rates across groups (CTRL: 11.4%; IN: 14.8%; OUT: 12.5%).
Participants were retained only if they contributed at least 10 valid trials per outcome feedback and at least 30 feedback trials overall.
The FRN was quantified over frontocentral electrodes Fz, FC1, FC2, and Cz using the mean peak-to-mean peak measure.
For each trial, activity was averaged across available electrodes in this region of interest.
The analysis window was defined from the grand-average waveform collapsed across groups, sessions, and outcome feedbacks.
The preceding positive peak (P2) was identified within the 150-220 ms window and quantified as the mean amplitude in a ±20 ms window around it.
The FRN local minimum was identified within the 220-300 ms window and quantified as the mean amplitude in a ±20 ms window around it.
Trial-level FRN amplitude was computed as the FRN-window mean minus the P2-window mean, such that more negative values indicate a stronger downward deflection relative to the preceding positivity.
For time-frequency analyses, cleaned continuous data were filtered between 1 and 40 Hz and segmented into feedback-locked epochs from -2 to 2 s.

Time-frequency representations were computed at the single-trial level using Morlet wavelets with 40 logarithmically spaced frequencies from 1 to 40 Hz, with the number of cycles increasing logarithmically from 1 to 14.
Power was z-score baseline-normalized relative to the -1 to 0 s pre-feedback interval and cropped to -2 to 2 s.
Time-frequency windows were defined from the grand-average activity collapsed across groups, sessions, and outcome feedbacks.
Analyses focused on frontocentral electrodes Fz, FC1, FC2, and Cz.
Delta power was extracted between 1 and 3.5 Hz and theta power between 3.5 and 8 Hz, both from 100 to 700 ms after feedback onset.
Automated epoch rejection for the time-frequency epochs used the same procedure as for the ERP analyses.
On average, 11.3% of time-frequency epochs used for delta and theta were rejected across sessions (CTRL: 10.9%; IN: 11.7%; OUT: 11.0%).

text.text: Models were fitted to trial-by-trial choice and outcome data from the probabilistic bandit task.
For each model, three Markov chain Monte Carlo chains were run for 4,000 iterations per chain, including 1,000 burn-in iterations.
All models were estimated using the default priors implemented in hBayesDM, with each parameter transformed to its bounded scale.

Seven reinforcementlearning models were evaluated: bandit2arm_delta, banditNarm_2par_lapse, banditNarm_4par, banditNarm_delta, banditNarm_lapse, banditNarm_lapse_decay, and banditNarm_singleA_lapse (Supplementary Table S5-1).

text.text: These models differed in the number of free parameters and assumptions regarding learning from reward and punishment outcomes, choice stochasticity, and decay of unchosen option values.
Depending on model specification, parameters included reward sensitivity (R), punishment sensitivity (P), reward learning rate (Arew), punishment learning rate (Apun), lapse rate (ξ), and decay.
Following Aylward et al. (2019), behavioural data from each Group (Control, Incoming, Outgoing) and Session (S1, S2) were initially fitted separately using independent hierarchical priors.
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr">Aylward et al. (2019)</ref>, behavioural data from each Group (Control, Incoming, Outgoing) and Session (S1, S2) were initially fitted separately using independent hierarchical priors.

text.text: This approach minimizes hierarchical shrinkage across groups and sessions, allowing potential between-group and longitudinal differences to emerge without partial pooling.

To assess the robustness of findings to prior specification, the best-performing models were subsequently re-estimated using alternative hierarchical prior structures based on pooled datasets across (a) groups, (b) sessions, and (c) groups and sessions simultaneously.
LOOIC values indicate better expected out-of-sample predictive performance.
The winning model was identified as the model with the lowest average LOOIC across the six group-bysession datasets (Control S1, Control S2, Incoming S1, Incoming S2, Outgoing S1, and Outgoing S2).

Figure1: Overview of the probabilistic Bandit Task.
Each trial began with a fixation cross (800-1200 ms), followed by the presentation of two slot machines.
Participants had up to 4 s to choose one option.
The selected slot machine remained on the screen for 1 s.
After another fixation cross, feedback was presented for 1 s, indicating either a monetary gain (+€0.25), a monetary loss (-€0.25), or a missed response ("Too late!").
A second fixation cross (800-1200 ms) separated consecutive trials.
The task consisted of five blocks of 25 trials, with reward contingencies reversing between blocks, requiring participants to learn and continuously update the most advantageous choice.
